claims.text: At 500–600 °C, FeNiCrCoCu coating wear resistance is primarily governed by formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer originates preferentially at nanoscale grain boundaries.
The oxide layer acts as a sacrificial barrier during sliding contact.
The oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and slows wear progression.
The baseline as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has a conventional nanocrystalline grain structure.
The baseline as-deposited coating has a uniform composition.
Adjusting deposition and post-deposition thermal treatment can produce a finer grain structure than the baseline condition.
Rapid thermal annealing can nucleate dispersed oxide precursor phases in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Increased grain-boundary density accelerates oxide nucleation and growth at elevated temperature.
The grain-boundary-facilitated oxide becomes continuous and adherent during high-temperature exposure and wear.
The continuous oxide layer limits plastic deformation during sliding.
The continuous oxide layer reduces abrasive wear.
Refined-grain coatings will form a more uniform and stable oxide layer than untreated baseline coatings.
Refined-grain coatings will exhibit lower wear rates than untreated baseline coatings at 500–600 °C under identical loading.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to sliding or contact wear at approximately 500–600 °C.
Behavior outside 500–600 °C or under drastically different loading conditions is not predicted by the hypothesis.
A lack of improved wear resistance and oxide-layer characteristics in refined-grain coatings relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of correlation between measurable oxide formation and improved wear behavior would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
